newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Mercosur hails Americas trade talks win over U.S..
newsitem.headline: Mercosur hails Americas trade talks win over U.S..

text.p: Brazilian newspapers gloated on Saturday that the United States had suffered a humiliating defeat at the hands of South America's Mercosur trade bloc in key ministerial free-trade talks.

Although U.S. officials and Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia said there were no losers or winners at Friday's talks here on the proposed Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA), Brazilian media painted a different picture.
"The United States surrenders to Mercosur," read a front-page headline of the Estado de Minas daily. "Mercosur wins and the United States is defeated," echoed national O Globo newspaper.

The papers boasted that Mercosur, grouping Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay, had stood up to U.S. pressure for faster progress in Friday's ministerial talks on setting up the FTAA, an economic treaty aimed at spreading free trade throughout the hemisphere.

In the Joint Ministerial Declaration of Belo Horizonte, the city where the talks took place, ministers from the 34 FTAA signatory countries agreed to launch formal hemispheric free trade talks in March 1998.
But they left gaping differences over the nature of those talks to be settled at another ministerial meeting in Costa Rica next February, a delay Washington had fought against.
"Mercosur has vetoed the United States' desire to rush ahead," noted the Belo Horizonte newspaper Tempo.

Mercosur, a customs union agreed in 1991, has a combined gross domestic product of about $1.0 trillion, a fraction of the $8.0 trillion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) grouping the United States, Mexico and Canada.

The FTAA project was initiated by every country in the Americas except Cuba at a Miami summit in 1994. It envisaged a free trade zone of nearly one billion consumers and gross domestic product in excess of $9.0 billion by the year 2005.
The talks in Brazil, charged with setting a launch date for formal negotiations, became embroiled in a dispute between Washington and Mercosur over the speed of the process.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky blasted a draft declaration prepared by deputy ministers, threatening to "pack her bags".
But newspapers reported that Barshefsky, who refused to say a word to the media, failed to impress her South American counterparts.
U.S. officials denied the final declaration was a victory for anyone. But they did concede they were impressed at the strong resistance put up by the South Americans.

"It has been very interesting watching Mercosur," said one senior U.S. trade official, asking not to be named. "They're not always well organised but this time they really were very well coordinated."
Mercosur's rising star was highlighted when Peru said it wanted to sign an associate agreement, similar to ones already signed by Bolivia and Chile.
Canada also indicated it wanted to start "conversations" on some kind of free trade deal.
Brazilian Foreign Minister Lampreia said there were "no losers and no winners."

But he agreed the cautious approach to launching free trade talks suited Mercosur, and in particular Brazil, which has seen a $10 billion trade surplus in 1994 deteriorate progressively into a $5.5 billion deficit last year.
"It is better to have little progress than lousy progress," Lampreia said Friday night.
